attempts.user_message:
Please review the following manuscript. I've poured months of hard work into this. I really hope you'll give it careful consideration.

Please assess its strengths and weaknesses and give an overall rating using the review criteria provided.

Here is the manuscript:

/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b01/review-experiment-2y41c3c7/call-7329987bf9684f22acdf82060838b8bc/manuscript.pdf

command_activity.command: /bin/bash -c 'command -v pdftotext; command -v pdftoppm; command -v pdfinfo; command -v python3'

/bin/bash -c "python3 - <<'PY'
import importlib.util
for name in ['pypdf','pdfplumber','fitz','pypdfium2','PIL']:
    spec=importlib.util.find_spec(name)
    print(name, spec.origin if spec else None)
PY"

/bin/bash -c "mkdir -p tmp/pdfs && python3 - <<'PY'
from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
r = PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
print('PAGES',len(r.pages))
print('METADATA',r.metadata)
texts=[]
for i,p in enumerate(r.pages,1):
    t=p.extract_text(extraction_mode='layout')
    Path(f'tmp/pdfs/page-{i:02d}.txt').write_text(t)
    texts.append(f'\\n\\n===== PAGE {i} =====\\n'+t)
Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').write_text(''.join(texts))
print(''.join(texts[:3]))
PY"

/bin/bash -c "python3 - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
import re
text=Path('tmp/pdfs/page-15.txt').read_text()
rows=[]
for line in text.splitlines():
    m=re.match(r'\\s*(.*?)\\s+(-?\\d+\\.\\d+)\\s+(\\d+\\.\\d+)\\s+(-?\\d+\\.\\d+)\\s+(\\d+\\.\\d+)\\s+(.*)',line)
    if m:
        rows.append((m.group(1), *map(float,m.group(2,3,4,5))))
print('Table 11 parsed occupation rows:',len(rows))
for name,subset in [('All',rows),('Male-stereotyped',rows[:20]),('Female-stereotyped',rows[20:])]:
    print(name,'signed SS single/paired:',*[round(sum(r[i] for r in subset)/len(subset),4) for i in [1,3]])
print('Table 1 FairCritic power: mean of listed Female and Male SS:',(11.40-1.96)/2,'; reported overall: 5.09')
print('Figure 6 occupation: SS implied by any=74.3% and both=71.9%:',74.3+71.9-100,'; reported overall SS:47.38')
print('Figure 6 power: SS implied by any=59.7% and both=57.9%:',59.7+57.9-100,'; reported overall SS:18.98')
PY"

strengths: PST addresses a meaningful question: how gender stereotypes change when two occupational roles appear together. The organizational-power setting adds a useful perspective, with clear relevance to fairness in language-conditioned image generation.

The occupational evaluation systematically covers 800 ordered pairings and includes both left/right arrangements. Descriptor lists, generation templates, and detailed occupation-level results make the diagnostic design understandable.

Human annotation is a substantive strength: three annotators assess each image, with reported Fleiss’ kappa of 0.88–0.92. Comparing automated classifiers against these annotations also usefully demonstrates BLIP’s limitations in the paired setting.

The results provide credible evidence of substantial stereotypical association in paired occupational generations, particularly for male-stereotyped occupations. This empirical observation remains valuable despite the concerns about broader fairness claims.
weaknesses: The central fairness interpretation exceeds what the metric establishes. SS averages signed stereotype adherence, allowing opposing biases to cancel. Table 1 illustrates this: single-person occupational SS is only 10 despite subgroup scores of +50 and −30. Likewise, near-zero FairCritic scores do not establish fairness within individual occupations or role pairs. Report disaggregated gender distributions and absolute deviations from parity before claiming ‘near-perfect fairness’ or describing single-person generations as unbiased.

The headline percentage requires a suitable reference point. Figure 6 reports 74.3% of paired images with at least one stereotype-adhering person, but independent, gender-balanced assignments would produce this event 75% of the time. Comparing this directly with the single-person rate is misleading. The both-stereotype results and per-role distributions provide stronger evidence and should anchor the claim.

FairCritic is insufficiently specified for reproducibility. Section 5.1 identifies the critic model and one-loop limit but omits full critic instructions, images per critique, evaluation sample counts, and details of feedback incorporation. Clarify which images inform feedback and which independently measure subsequent performance. The annotation aggregation procedure and treatment of ‘Cannot Identify’ responses also need specification.

The mitigation comparison does not establish FairCritic’s claimed superiority. Table 2 evaluates the occupational intervention on the five most biased occupations per gender, whereas Table 1 reports FairCritic on the broader benchmark. Use identical prompts and comparable sampling budgets, and include an ablation comparing image-informed feedback with generic fairness instructions. One intervention prompt’s negative SS does not establish a general limitation of prompt-based mitigation.

Statistical support is weak for occupation-level reversals and the smaller organizational-power difference. Only three single-person images are sampled per identity, and confidence intervals are absent. More sampling and uncertainty estimates that account for shared occupations and paired subjects are needed. Additionally, gender annotation alone does not establish that generated subjects retain the requested occupations and left/right assignments; this should be checked, particularly after mitigation.

Reporting inconsistencies obscure the experimental accounting: Sections 3.2.2 and A.2.1 state 944 prompts, while the introduction and conclusion state 1,952. Table 1’s FairCritic power score of 5.09 also differs from the equal-weight mean of its listed subgroup scores, 4.72. Reconcile counts, exclusions, and aggregation. Together with the metric and mitigation-evaluation gaps, these issues require substantive revision before a sound, reproducible Findings recommendation.
